children.author: xyzzy123
children.text:
Most of the world does NOT optimise for efficiency, particularly at the big end. Really big hyperscale companies (and some startups) are unusual because they at least sort of try, most of the world is not even trying.

The org structure is optimised to reduce or even minimise individual agency, explicitly at the cost of efficiency.

Teams have fiefdoms, private repos that the rest of the org can't see. You are not granted permission to see what permissions you have. Byzantine department structures. Shipping "hello world" to production takes 3-6 months and nobody can imagine it working any other way.

There's actually no central directory of teams or processes. To get anything meaningful done, you need the co-operation of maybe 8 teams but there's no consistent way to engage them all. You have to negotiate with them all in different ways, they're like little warlords, sitting and guarding access to some vital resource you need. They have established a ticket-based interface with a 7 day SLA on top of a perfectly good vending API that could do what you need in seconds. Sometimes a blocking team has a 3 month backlog so your project will just have to wait.

Everything is always in the process of being restructured, so no end to end 6 month process happens the same way every time.

These organisations could use AI to run the end to end process in minutes. Heck, they could just put APIs on top of what they already have. But the way they WANT to use it is to keep doing what they're doing but with EVEN MORE form filling and paperwork.

You would think they would get outcompeted, but no. The "IT organisation" sits like a brain slug on top of an enterprise with substantial regulatory, capital and execution moats.

Big cuts of course do happen in these places, but it's often for optics (we need to signal that we care about efficiency, and AI is a great excuse). But you can't protect yourself by being efficient and good at your job, because the cuts were not about output.

Yeah, but that still doesn’t mean there aren’t theoretical bugs. Testing every input would effectively mean testing every stimulus, which is combinatorially impossible. You might still have subtle timing bugs, bugs with very uncommon instruction sequences etc.

But my point was exactly that the (extremely vastly) smaller subset of tests that you performed is more than enough to proclaim a CPU to be “working”.

This is a case where we basically did test it on everything! Because the emulation community maintains conformance tests with over 3k of golden instructions. (And this is why Opus was able to so effectively build it; it found the tests)

Do you test every possible input/output combination on any CPU?

No, because that would be impossible.

You perform a series of more specific tests. In this case, it's "working" in so far as that Super Mario Bros. appears to be playable, for example.

Does not mean that it behaves perfectly according to some spec, or identical to another CPU (like the NES's 6502), of course, but it's clearly a working CPU to some 6502-compatible extent.

I'm doing something similar but not for an emulator, using tests other projects in a similar space use to validate things.

I also know a friend that feeds Claude Gherkin formatted test criteria, and apparently that yields insanely good Claude output.

A couple thoughts on the process here…

First off, Opus 5.5 built working weights and code with only two prompts:

1. Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.

It returned charts well illustrating any model would be _slow_. But it's still fun, so the second prompt was:

2. I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.

Now while this was an _epic_ run by Opus (5.5 is a crazy capable model), this is a surprisingly well-structured challenge.

There is a long-lived and incredible community of classic gaming emulation work online for it to reference. And that community has created…conformance tests! Opus found them and built against one, that has >3k golden instructions: https://github.com/christopherpow/nes-test-roms/blob/master/...

Also, there is the original Qwenputer repo that Opus used to drive the weight writing. That was essential.

But this is a great example of what these models can do with proper reference materials, great specs, conformance tests, and clear direction.
